name: Clamp to Range
background: Clamping means forcing a number to stay inside an allowed window. If the number is below the low bound it becomes the low bound; if it is above the high bound it becomes the high bound; otherwise it is left alone. Clamping 20 into the window [0, 10] gives 10.
task: Read N integers and clamp each one into the inclusive range [L, R]. Print the resulting N integers in order.
input_format:
Line 1: N, L, R (space-separated).
Line 2: N space-separated integers.

name: Residue Reduction
background: The residue of a number modulo M is the remainder left after dividing by M, always reported as a value from 0 to M-1. Note that negative numbers still get a non-negative residue: -1 modulo 5 is 4, because -1 = (-1 x 5) + 4.
task: Read N integers and replace each one with its non-negative residue modulo M. Print the resulting sequence.
input_format:
Line 1: N, M (space-separated).
Line 2: N space-separated integers.

name: Truncated Quotient
background: Truncating division throws away the fractional part and always rounds toward zero, never away from it. So 7 divided by 2 truncates to 3, and -7 divided by 2 truncates to -3 (not -4). This differs from the floor division used by default in some languages.
task: Read N integers and replace each one with the quotient of dividing it by K, truncated toward zero. Print the resulting N integers.
input_format:
Line 1: N, K (space-separated).
Line 2: N space-separated integers.

name: Sign Map
background: The sign of a number records only its direction, not its size. Negative numbers have sign -1, zero has sign 0, and positive numbers have sign 1. So the list [-9, 0, 2] maps to [-1, 0, 1].
task: Read N integers and output the sign of each one (-1, 0, or 1) in the original order.
input_format:
Line 1: N.
Line 2: N space-separated integers.

name: Absolute Cap
background: The absolute value of a number is its distance from zero, so it is never negative: the absolute value of -8 is 8. Capping at C means any value larger than C is replaced by C. Combining both, -8 with a cap of 5 becomes 5.
task: Read N integers. Replace each with its absolute value, capped at C. Print the resulting N non-negative integers.
input_format:
Line 1: N, C (space-separated).
Line 2: N space-separated integers.

name: Reverse the Line
background: Reversing a sequence means reading it back to front, so the last item becomes first and the first becomes last. Reversing [1, 2, 3] gives [3, 2, 1]. Nothing is added or removed, only repositioned.
task: Read N integers and print them in reverse order.
input_format:
Line 1: N.
Line 2: N space-separated integers.

name: Rotate Right
background: A right rotation slides every element K places toward the end, and anything pushed off the end wraps back around to the front. Rotating [1, 2, 3, 4] right by 1 gives [4, 1, 2, 3]. The elements keep their relative order; only their starting point shifts.
task: Read N integers and print the sequence after rotating it right by K positions.
input_format:
Line 1: N, K (space-separated).
Line 2: N space-separated integers.

name: Shuffle the Halves
background: A riffle shuffle splits a deck into two halves and alternates cards from each. Here the first half and second half are woven together the same way: first item of half one, first item of half two, second of half one, and so on. [1, 2, 3, 4] becomes [1, 3, 2, 4].
task: Read N integers (N is even), split them into two equal halves, and print the two halves interleaved.
input_format:
Line 1: N (always even).
Line 2: N space-separated integers.

name: Evens Take the Front
background: Positions here are counted starting at 1, so the 1st, 3rd, 5th items sit at odd positions and the 2nd, 4th, 6th sit at even positions. This is about where an item sits, not whether the number itself is even. For [9, 8, 7], position 2 holds the value 8.
task: Read N integers. Print all elements at even positions first (in increasing position order), followed by all elements at odd positions (also in increasing position order).
input_format:
Line 1: N.
Line 2: N space-separated integers.

name: Swap Neighbours
background: The sequence is walked in pairs from the left: items 1 and 2 trade places, then items 3 and 4, and so on. If the count is odd there is no partner left for the final item, so it stays exactly where it is. [1, 2, 3] becomes [2, 1, 3].
task: Read N integers and swap each adjacent pair (1st with 2nd, 3rd with 4th, and so on). If N is odd the last element stays in place. Print the resulting sequence.
input_format:
Line 1: N.
Line 2: N space-separated integers.

name: Negate the Segment
background: A segment is a run of consecutive positions described by a start L and an end R. Both endpoints are included, so the segment [2, 4] covers positions 2, 3 and 4. Negating a number flips its sign, turning 5 into -5 and -5 into 5.
task: Read N integers and negate every element inside the inclusive segment [L, R]. Print the resulting array in order.
input_format:
Line 1: N, L, R (space-separated).
Line 2: N space-separated integers.
constraints:
N: 1-100
L, R: 1-based, with 1 <= L <= R <= N
values: -10000 to 10000

name: Reverse a Substring
background: A substring is a stretch of consecutive characters inside a longer word, marked here by a start position L and an end position R with both ends included. Only that stretch is flipped back to front; every character outside it stays untouched. In 'abcde', reversing positions 2 to 4 gives 'adcbe'.
task: Read a lowercase string and two positions L and R. Reverse the substring covering positions L through R (inclusive) and print the modified string.
input_format:
Line 1: the string S (lowercase letters only).
Line 2: L, R (space-separated).
constraints:
length of S: 1-100
L, R: 1-based, with 1 <= L <= R <= length of S

name: Overwrite then Total
background: Every position from L to R (both included) is overwritten with the same value V, wiping out whatever was there before. Afterwards the whole array is added up. Overwriting positions 2 to 3 of [1, 2, 3, 4] with 0 leaves [1, 0, 0, 4], which totals 5.
task: Read N integers, replace every element in the inclusive segment [L, R] with V, then print the sum of the whole array.
input_format:
Line 1: N, L, R, V (space-separated).
Line 2: N space-separated integers.

name: Flip and Count Ones
background: A binary array holds only 0s and 1s. Flipping a bit swaps it to the other value: 0 becomes 1 and 1 becomes 0. Only bits inside the inclusive window [L, R] are flipped, then the total number of 1s left in the whole array is reported.
task: Read N bits and flip every bit in the inclusive segment [L, R]. Print how many 1s the array contains afterwards.
input_format:
Line 1: N, L, R (space-separated).
Line 2: N space-separated bits, each 0 or 1.
constraints:
N: 1-100
L, R: 1-based, with 1 <= L <= R <= N
bits: 0 or 1

name: Zero Out and Report
background: Every position from L to R (both included) is set to 0. An entry only counts as changed if it was something other than 0 to begin with, since setting a 0 to 0 changes nothing. Zeroing positions 1 to 3 of [0, 4, 0] changes just one entry.
task: Read N integers and set every element in the inclusive segment [L, R] to 0. Print how many array entries actually changed value.
input_format:
Line 1: N, L, R (space-separated).
Line 2: N space-separated integers.
constraints:
N: 1-100
L, R: 1-based, with 1 <= L <= R <= N
values: -10000 to 10000

name: Above the Bar
background: Filtering keeps only the entries that pass a test and discards the rest, without reordering anything that survives. Here the test is 'strictly greater than T', so a score exactly equal to T does not pass. If nothing passes, the output line is simply empty.
task: Read N scores and print only those strictly greater than T, in their original order. If no score qualifies, print an empty line.
input_format:
Line 1: N, T (space-separated).
Line 2: N space-separated integers.

name: Even IDs Only
background: A number is even when dividing it by 2 leaves no remainder, so 4 and 100 are even while 7 is not. The surviving IDs must stay in the order they arrived. If none of them are even, the output line is empty.
task: Read N positive integer IDs and print only the even ones, preserving the original order. If there are no even IDs, print an empty line.
input_format:
Line 1: N.
Line 2: N space-separated positive integers.

name: Divisible Survivors
background: A number is divisible by K when dividing it by K leaves a remainder of exactly zero. Note that 0 is divisible by every K, since 0 divided by anything leaves no remainder. Order is preserved among the numbers that pass.
task: Read N integers and print those divisible by K, in their original order. If none are divisible, print an empty line.
input_format:
Line 1: N, K (space-separated).
Line 2: N space-separated integers.

name: Pick the Category
background: Each item carries a label saying which category it belongs to. Only items whose label matches the requested category exactly are kept, and matching is case-sensitive so 'Fruit' and 'fruit' are different labels. Kept items appear in the order they were listed.
task: Read N item/category pairs and a target category C. Print the item names whose category equals C, preserving input order. If no item matches, print an empty line.
input_format:
Line 1: N.
Next N lines: item_name and category, separated by a space.
Last line: the target category C.
constraints:
N: 1-100
names and categories: 1-20 letters, case-sensitive, no spaces

name: Vowel Starters
background: The vowels are a, e, i, o and u. Only the very first letter of each word is examined, and the check ignores capitalisation so 'Apple' and 'apple' both start with a vowel. The letter y is not treated as a vowel here.
task: Read N words and print only those starting with a vowel (a, e, i, o, u; case-insensitive), keeping their original order. If none start with a vowel, print an empty line.
input_format:
Line 1: N.
Line 2: N space-separated words.

N: 1-100
words: 1-20 English letters, may be upper or lower case

name: Count the Runs
background: A run is a maximal block of neighbouring items that are all identical. The sequence [1, 1, 2, 2, 2, 1] contains three runs: two 1s, then three 2s, then a single 1. Note the last run counts even though the same value appeared earlier, because runs are about adjacency.
task: Read N integers and print the number of runs, where a run is a maximal block of consecutive equal values.
input_format:
Line 1: N.
Line 2: N space-separated integers.

name: Spell Out the Runs
background: Run-length encoding rewrites a word by naming each block of repeated letters once, followed by how many times it repeats. The word 'aab' becomes 'a 2 b 1'. Blocks are read strictly left to right, and a letter that reappears later starts a brand new block.
task: Read a lowercase string and print its run-length encoding as 'letter count' pairs separated by single spaces, in left-to-right order.
input_format: Line 1: the string S (lowercase letters only).

name: Longest Colour Streak
background: A streak is a block of neighbouring tiles sharing the same colour. The goal is the single longest such block. If two different streaks are tied at the same maximum length, the one that starts earliest (furthest left) wins.
task: Read N colour names describing a strip and print the colour of the longest consecutive run followed by that run's length, separated by a space. If several runs tie, choose the leftmost.
input_format:
Line 1: N.
Line 2: N space-separated colour names.

name: Compress the Bits
background: A binary string is squeezed into segments written as value:length, listing each block of identical bits once. The string '0011100' compresses to '0:2,1:3,0:2'. Segments are joined by commas with no spaces anywhere in the output.
task: Read a binary string and print its compression as segments 'v:l' joined by commas with no spaces, in left-to-right order.
input_format: Line 1: the binary string B (characters 0 and 1 only).

name: Bracketed Encoding
background: Each block of repeated values is written as a bracketed pair holding the value and the block length, like (7,3) for three consecutive 7s. There are no spaces inside a pair, and pairs are separated by exactly one space.
task: Read N non-negative integers and print their run-length encoding as pairs written (v,L), with no spaces inside a pair and a single space between pairs.
input_format:
Line 1: N.
Line 2: N space-separated integers.

name: Odd Gets A, Even Gets B
background: Positions are counted starting at 1, so the 1st, 3rd and 5th slots are odd and the 2nd, 4th and 6th are even. This depends purely on where a number sits, not on whether the number itself is odd or even. Every odd slot gains A and every even slot gains B.
task: Read N integers. Add A to every element at an odd position and B to every element at an even position. Print the resulting array.
input_format:
Line 1: N, A, B (space-separated).
Line 2: N space-separated integers.
constraints:
N: 1-100
A, B: -1000 to 1000
positions are 1-based
values: -10000 to 10000

name: Zigzag Case
background: Positions here start at 0, so the very first character sits at position 0 which is even. Even positions are forced to uppercase and odd positions to lowercase, regardless of how the letter was originally typed. 'hello' becomes 'HeLlO'.
task: Read a string of letters. Convert characters at even positions to uppercase and characters at odd positions to lowercase. Print the transformed string.
input_format: Line 1: the string S (English letters only).

name: Alternating Total
background: Positions start at 1. Everything sitting at an odd position is added and everything at an even position is subtracted, giving a single running total. For [5, 3, 2] the result is 5 - 3 + 2, which is 4.
task: Read N integers and print the alternating sum: the total of elements at odd positions minus the total of elements at even positions.
input_format:
Line 1: N.
Line 2: N space-separated integers.

name: Flip Every Other Word
background: Word positions start at 0, so the first word sits at position 0 which is even and is left alone. Words at odd positions have their letters written back to front. The words themselves never change places, only their internal spelling.
task: Read N words. Reverse the letters of each word at an odd position (0-based) and leave words at even positions unchanged. Print the words in order.
input_format:
Line 1: N.
Line 2: N space-separated words.
constraints:
N: 1-100
positions are 0-based
words: 1-20 lowercase letters

name: Square the Odds, Cube the Evens
background: Positions start at 1. Squaring means multiplying a number by itself once (3 squared is 9) and cubing means multiplying it by itself twice (3 cubed is 27). Squares are never negative, but cubes keep the sign of the original number: -2 cubed is -8.
task: Read N integers. Replace each element at an odd position with its square and each element at an even position with its cube. Print the updated array.
input_format:
Line 1: N.
Line 2: N space-separated integers.

name: Coldest Day
background: Scanning for a minimum means tracking the smallest value seen so far. A witness is the extra detail reported alongside it, here the position where it lives. If the same low reading occurs more than once, the earliest one wins, so positions are compared as a tie-breaker.
task: Read N daily temperatures. Print the minimum temperature followed by the 1-based index of its first occurrence, separated by a space.
input_format:
Line 1: N.
Line 2: N space-separated integers.

name: Last Peak Price
background: The maximum is the largest value in the list. When that same peak value shows up several times, the required answer is the latest position where it appears, not the first. Positions are counted starting at 1.
task: Read N stock prices in chronological order. Print the 1-based index of the LAST occurrence of the maximum price. Output the index only.
input_format:
Line 1: N.
Line 2: N space-separated integers.

name: Top Score
background: The highest score is simply the largest number in the list. Because only the value is reported and not who achieved it, ties make no difference to the answer: several contestants sharing the top score still produce the same single number.
task: Read N contest scores and print the highest score value.
input_format:
Line 1: N.
Line 2: N space-separated integers.

name: Latest Low Reading
background: Indices here start at 0, so the first sensor reading sits at index 0. The task looks for the smallest reading, and when that value repeats it reports the greatest index holding it rather than the first. The index is printed before the reading itself.
task: Read N sensor readings. Print the 0-based index of the LAST occurrence of the minimum reading, followed by that minimum reading, separated by a space.
input_format:
Line 1: N.
Line 2: N space-separated integers.

name: Highest Point on the Trail
background: The maximum is the largest elevation recorded. The position reported alongside it is counted starting at 1. When the same peak elevation is measured more than once, the earliest position is the one that is reported.
task: Read N elevation measurements. Print the maximum elevation followed by the 1-based position of its first occurrence, separated by a space.
input_format:
Line 1: N.
Line 2: N space-separated integers.

name: Count the Rich Accounts
background: Counting means reporting how many entries pass a test, not the entries themselves. The test here is 'strictly greater than T', so a balance exactly equal to T is not counted. If nothing passes, the answer is 0.
task: Read N account balances and print how many of them are strictly greater than T.
input_format:
Line 1: N, T (space-separated).
Line 2: N space-separated integers.

name: Count the Odd Days
background: A number is odd when dividing it by 2 leaves a remainder of 1. Negative numbers can be odd too: -3 is odd because it is not evenly divisible by 2. Zero is even, so it is never counted.
task: Read N daily step counts and print how many of them are odd numbers.
input_format:
Line 1: N.
Line 2: N space-separated integers.

name: Count the Freezing Readings
background: A reading is below freezing when it is strictly less than zero. Exactly 0.0 degrees is not below zero and so is not counted. Readings are decimal values, so -0.1 counts even though it is only just negative.
task: Read N Celsius temperature readings and print how many of them are below 0.
input_format:
Line 1: N.
Line 2: N space-separated decimal numbers.
constraints:
N: 1-100
readings: -100.0 to 100.0, given with one decimal place

name: Count the Divisible Codes
background: A code is divisible by K when dividing it by K leaves a remainder of exactly zero. Zero itself is divisible by every K. Only the count is reported, not the codes.
task: Read N product codes and print how many are divisible by K.
input_format:
Line 1: N, K (space-separated).
Line 2: N space-separated integers.

name: Count the Capitals
background: An uppercase letter is one of the 26 characters A through Z. Digits, punctuation, spaces and lowercase letters all fail the test. The string may mix any of these together.
task: Read a line of text and print how many characters are uppercase English letters (A-Z).
input_format: Line 1: the string S.
constraints:
length of S: 1-100
S may contain letters, digits, spaces and symbols
test7_input: aA bB cC dD eE fF

name: Positive Odd-Position Sum
background: Two filters apply at once: the element must sit at an odd position (positions start at 1) and it must be strictly positive. An element failing either test contributes nothing. If no element passes both, the total is 0.
task: Read N integers and print the sum of all positive elements located at odd positions (1-based). If no element qualifies, print 0.
input_format:
Line 1: N.
Line 2: N space-separated integers.

name: Every Third Bit
background: Only the bits sitting at positions 3, 6, 9 and so on are examined; positions start at 1. Their product is 1 only when every one of them is 1, because a single 0 drags the product to 0. If the sequence is too short to have any such position, the answer is 1, the multiplicative identity.
task: Read N bits and compute the product of all bits at positions that are multiples of 3. Print 1 if that product equals 1, otherwise 0. If no such position exists, print 1.
input_format:
Line 1: N.
Line 2: N space-separated bits, each 0 or 1.

name: Digit Sums of Multiples
background: Only numbers divisible by K are considered. For each of those, its decimal digits are added up: the digit sum of 45 is 4 + 5 = 9. All those digit sums are then totalled. Zero is divisible by every K and has a digit sum of 0.
task: Read N integers and print the total of the decimal digit-sums of every element divisible by K. If no element is divisible by K, print 0.
input_format:
Line 1: N, K (space-separated).
Line 2: N space-separated integers.

name: Within Tolerance
background: An element is within tolerance when its distance from zero is at most T, meaning both x and -x are compared against the same bound. The boundary is included, so a value of exactly T or exactly -T qualifies. Both how many qualified and their total are reported.
task: Read N integers and count how many satisfy |value| <= T, also computing the sum of those values. Print the count and the sum separated by a space. If none qualify, print '0 0'.
input_format:
Line 1: N, T (space-separated).
Line 2: N space-separated integers.

name: Heads and Even
background: Each coin carries both a value and a face label, H for heads or T for tails. A coin counts only if it is showing heads AND its value is an even number; failing either condition excludes it. Zero is even, so a heads coin worth 0 qualifies but adds nothing.
task: Read N coin values and a label string of H and T characters. Print the sum of values for coins labelled 'H' whose value is even. If no coin matches, print 0.
input_format:
Line 1: N.
Line 2: N space-separated non-negative integers.
Line 3: a string of N characters, each 'H' or 'T'.
constraints:
N: 1-100
values: 0-1000000
label string length equals N

name: Find the Target
background: A linear scan walks the array from left to right and stops at the very first item that matches. Later matches are irrelevant once one has been found. Positions are counted starting at 1, and a missing target is reported as -1.
task: Read N integers and a target T. Print the 1-based index of the first element equal to T, or -1 if T does not appear.
input_format:
Line 1: N, T (space-separated).
Line 2: N space-separated integers.

name: First Tall Person
background: The queue is scanned from the front backwards, stopping at the first person strictly taller than H; someone exactly H tall does not qualify. Positions start at 0, so the person at the front is at position 0. If nobody is tall enough the word NONE is printed instead.
task: Read N heights in queue order (front to back) and a threshold H. Print the 0-based position of the first person strictly taller than H, or NONE if nobody qualifies.
input_format:
Line 1: N, H (space-separated).
Line 2: N space-separated integers.
constraints:
N: 1-100
positions are 0-based
H and heights: 1-300

name: Locate the Product Class
background: The shelf is read from left to right and the first position whose category matches the request is reported. Positions start at 1, which frees up 0 to mean 'not found anywhere on the shelf'.
task: Read N product category IDs along a shelf and a requested class C. Print the 1-based position of the first product whose category equals C, or 0 if no product matches.
input_format:
Line 1: N, C (space-separated).
Line 2: N space-separated integers.

name: First Passing Grade
background: Scores are read oldest to newest and the search stops at the first one that reaches the pass mark. 'At least P' includes P itself, so a score exactly equal to the pass mark counts as a pass. If the mark is never reached, the word NO is printed.
task: Read N exam scores in chronological order and a passing mark P. Print the 1-based index of the first score that is at least P, or NO if the mark is never reached.
input_format:
Line 1: N, P (space-separated).
Line 2: N space-separated integers.

name: First Upward Move
background: Neighbouring days are compared in pairs, looking for the first time the price goes strictly up from one day to the next. Equal prices do not count as an increase. The answer is the 1-based index of the earlier day in that pair, or -1 when prices never rise.
task: Read N daily stock prices in time order. Print the 1-based index i of the earliest adjacent pair where price[i] < price[i+1], or -1 if no such pair exists.
input_format:
Line 1: N.
Line 2: N space-separated integers.

name: Is It Sorted
background: A sequence is nondecreasing when every element is less than or equal to the one after it, so it never steps downward. Equal neighbours are allowed, meaning [2, 2, 5] is nondecreasing. A single element is trivially nondecreasing since there are no pairs to compare.
task: Read N integers and print YES if the sequence is nondecreasing, otherwise NO.
input_format:
Line 1: N.
Line 2: N space-separated integers.

name: Smooth Enough
background: The gap between two neighbours is the absolute difference between them, so direction does not matter: the gap between 5 and 9 is the same as between 9 and 5. The sequence passes only if every single adjacent gap is at most K. One bad gap is enough to fail.
task: Read N integers and a limit K. Print YES if every adjacent pair differs by at most K in absolute value, otherwise NO.
input_format:
Line 1: N, K (space-separated).
Line 2: N space-separated integers.

name: Perfect Alternation
background: A binary string alternates strictly when no two neighbouring characters are the same, producing patterns like 0101 or 1010. Any place where two identical bits sit side by side breaks the pattern. A single-character string alternates trivially.
task: Read a binary string and print YES if no two adjacent characters are equal, otherwise NO.
input_format: Line 1: the binary string S (characters 0 and 1 only).

name: Find a Close Pair
background: Neighbouring heights are compared in pairs, looking for one whose absolute difference is at most D. The boundary counts, so a difference of exactly D qualifies. When several pairs qualify, report the earliest one; the index printed is that of the left member of the pair.
task: Read N heights and a limit D. Print the smallest 1-based index i such that |h[i+1] - h[i]| <= D, or -1 if no adjacent pair is that close.
input_format:
Line 1: N, D (space-separated).
Line 2: N space-separated integers.

name: No Repeats Side by Side
background: The list is checked for two identical words sitting next to each other. A word may appear many times overall without breaking the rule, as long as its copies are never adjacent. If a violation exists, the 1-based index of the first (left) word of that pair is reported.
task: Read N words and verify that no two neighbouring words are equal. Print OK if the property holds, otherwise print the 1-based index i of the first position where w[i] equals w[i+1].
input_format:
Line 1: N.
Line 2: N space-separated words.

name: Best Two-Day Haul
background: Only pairs of days that sit next to each other are considered, never days further apart. Each pair's earnings are added together and the largest such total wins. Earnings can be negative, so the best total may still be a negative number.
task: Read N daily earnings in order and print the maximum sum of any two consecutive days.
input_format:
Line 1: N.
Line 2: N space-separated integers.

name: Steadiest Moment
background: Every neighbouring pair of readings has a gap, measured as an absolute difference so it is never negative. The smallest such gap marks the steadiest moment. If several pairs share that same smallest gap, the earliest one wins, and its left index is reported.
task: Read N temperature readings. Print the minimum absolute difference between adjacent readings, followed by the 1-based left index of the first pair achieving it, separated by a space.
input_format:
Line 1: N.
Line 2: N space-separated integers.

name: Strongest Adjacent Product
background: Each neighbouring pair of troop strengths is multiplied together and the largest product wins. Watch the signs: two negative numbers multiply to a positive, so a pair of large negatives can beat a pair of small positives. Products may be much larger than the inputs themselves.
task: Read N troop strengths along a line and print the largest product of any two adjacent strengths.
input_format:
Line 1: N.
Line 2: N space-separated integers.

name: Busiest Adjacent Window
background: Neighbouring timestamps are summed and the pair with the largest total is located. What gets reported is not the sum itself but the two positions involved, left one first, counted from 1. Ties are broken by choosing the pair with the smaller left index.
task: Read N timestamps in chronological order. Find the adjacent pair with the largest sum and print its two 1-based indices (left then right), separated by a space. If several pairs tie, choose the earliest left index.
input_format:
Line 1: N.
Line 2: N space-separated integers.

name: Closest to Cancelling Out
background: Two neighbouring voltages cancel out when they add to zero, so the pair whose sum is nearest to zero is wanted. The measure is the absolute value of the sum, meaning -2 and +2 are equally close. The two actual readings are printed, not their positions.
task: Read N sensor voltage readings. Find the adjacent pair whose values have the smallest absolute sum and print those two values (left then right), separated by a space. If several pairs tie, choose the earliest left index.
input_format:
Line 1: N.
Line 2: N space-separated integers.

name: Digit Census
background: A tally counts how many times each possible value shows up. Here all ten digits 0 through 9 are always reported in that fixed order, even the ones that never appear, which get a count of 0. The string '112' produces the tally 0 2 1 0 0 0 0 0 0 0.
task: Read a string of decimal digits and print ten integers: how many times each digit 0 through 9 appears, in that exact order.
input_format: Line 1: the string S (characters 0-9 only).

name: Letter Census
background: Every one of the 26 letters from a to z is reported in alphabetical order, including letters that never occur, which score 0. The output therefore always contains exactly 26 numbers no matter how short the input is.
task: Read a string of N lowercase letters and print 26 integers: the count of each letter from 'a' to 'z' in alphabetical order.
input_format:
Line 1: N.
Line 2: a string of exactly N lowercase letters.

name: Colour Census
background: The six colours are always reported in the fixed order red, orange, yellow, green, blue, purple, regardless of the order they appear in the input. Colours that never appear still get printed with a count of 0.
task: Read N colour names and print six integers: the count of each colour in the fixed order red, orange, yellow, green, blue, purple.
input_format:
Line 1: N.
Line 2: N space-separated colour names.

name: Weekday Census
background: The seven weekdays are always reported starting with Monday and ending with Sunday, no matter what order they arrived in. Days that never appear are printed as 0. Names are matched exactly, including their capital first letter.
task: Read N weekday names and print seven integers: the count of Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday, Friday, Saturday, Sunday in that order.

name: Rating Census
background: Ratings run from 1 to 5 and all five are always reported in increasing order, including any that nobody gave, which appear as 0. The output always contains exactly five numbers.
task: Read N ratings, each between 1 and 5, and print five integers: the frequency of ratings 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5 respectively.
input_format:
Line 1: N.
Line 2: N space-separated integers.

name: Most Popular Digit
background: Every digit from 0 to 9 is a candidate, and digits that never appear simply have a count of 0. The winner is whichever digit appears most often. When two or more digits are tied at the top, the smallest of those digits is chosen.
task: Read N digits and print the digit that appears most often. If several digits tie, print the smallest one among them.
input_format:
Line 1: N.
Line 2: N space-separated digits.

name: Least Popular Colour
background: All eight colours are candidates in the fixed order red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo, violet, brown, and a colour nobody voted for has a count of 0, which usually makes it the winner. The least frequent colour is wanted. Ties go to whichever colour comes first in that listed order.
task: Read N colour votes and print the least frequent colour. If several colours tie, print the one appearing earliest in the order red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo, violet, brown.

name: Most Common Rating
background: All five ratings from 1 to 5 are candidates, and a rating nobody gave counts as 0. The most common rating wins. Unusually, ties here are broken by choosing the HIGHEST tied rating rather than the lowest.
task: Read N ratings between 1 and 5 and print the most common rating. If there is a tie, print the highest rating among those tied.

Line 2: N space-separated integers.

name: Most Chosen Option
background: The four options A, B, C and D are all candidates, and an option nobody picked counts as 0. The option chosen most often wins, and when there is a tie the alphabetically smallest of the tied options is reported.
task: Read N multiple-choice answers, each one of A, B, C or D, and print the option that occurs most frequently. If there is a tie, print the alphabetically smallest tied option.

name: Exact Palindrome
background: A palindrome reads the same forwards and backwards, like 'level'. This check is case-sensitive, so 'Aba' is NOT a palindrome because the capital A does not match the lowercase a. An empty string counts as a palindrome, as does any single character.
task: Read a string S and print YES if it reads identically forwards and backwards (case-sensitive), otherwise NO.
input_format: Line 1: the string S (may be empty).
constraints:
length of S: 0-100
S contains English letters only

name: Palindrome After Cleaning
background: Before checking, every space and comma is stripped out of the text, leaving only the letters. The palindrome test then runs on that cleaned-up string. So 'ab, ba' cleans to 'abba', which reads the same both ways.
task: Read a line of text made of lowercase letters, spaces and commas. Remove all spaces and commas, then print YES if what remains is a palindrome, otherwise NO.
input_format: Line 1: the text T (lowercase letters, spaces and commas only).
test6_input: a man a plan a canal panama

name: Symmetric Array
background: An array is symmetric when the first element matches the last, the second matches the second-to-last, and so on inward. An array of length 0 or 1 is symmetric because there is nothing that can mismatch.
task: Read N integers and print YES if the array is symmetric (element i equals element N+1-i for every position), otherwise NO.
input_format:
Line 1: N.
Line 2: N space-separated integers (this line is empty when N is 0).

name: Case-Blind Palindrome
background: Every uppercase letter is first folded down to lowercase, while digits are left exactly as they are. The palindrome test then runs on that normalised string, so 'AbBa' passes because it becomes 'abba'.
task: Read a string of letters and digits. Convert all uppercase letters to lowercase, then print YES if the result reads the same forwards and backwards, otherwise NO.
input_format: Line 1: the string S (English letters and digits only).

name: Where It Breaks
background: The string is compared against its mirror image from the outside in: position 1 against the last position, position 2 against the second-to-last, and so on. If everything matches the answer is YES; otherwise the 1-based position of the leftmost mismatch is reported instead.
task: Read a string S. If S is a palindrome (case-sensitive), print YES. Otherwise print the 1-based index of the leftmost position whose character differs from its mirror position.
input_format: Line 1: the string S (may be empty).
constraints:
length of S: 0-100
S contains English letters only

name: Mirror Mismatches
background: Characters are paired up from the outside inward: the 1st with the last, the 2nd with the second-to-last, and so on. With an odd length the exact middle character has no partner and is simply ignored. The answer counts how many of those pairs disagree.
task: Read a string S and print how many mirror pairs (positions i and N+1-i) contain different characters.
input_format: Line 1: the string S.
constraints:
length of S: 1-100
S contains English letters only

name: Mirror Distance
background: Elements are paired from the outside inward, first with last and so on, and with an odd length the middle element is left out. For each pair the absolute difference is taken, so order within the pair does not matter, and all those differences are added up.
task: Read N integers and print the sum of |A[i] - A[N+1-i]| over all mirror pairs.
input_format:
Line 1: N.
Line 2: N space-separated integers.

name: List the Broken Mirrors
background: Bits are paired from the outside inward, and with an odd length the middle bit has no partner. Rather than counting the disagreeing pairs, this task lists the left-hand position of each one, in increasing order. If every pair agrees, the output line is empty.
task: Read a binary string B. Print the 1-based left-side indices i where B[i] differs from B[N+1-i], in increasing order, separated by spaces. If there are none, print an empty line.
input_format: Line 1: the binary string B (characters 0 and 1 only).

name: DNA Mirror Faults
background: A DNA string uses only the four letters A, C, G and T. Positions are paired from the outside inward, and an odd-length strand leaves its middle base unpaired. The answer is how many of those pairs hold different bases.
task: Read a DNA string D over the alphabet A, C, G, T. Print the number of mirror pairs (positions i and N+1-i) where the two bases differ.
input_format: Line 1: the DNA string D (characters A, C, G, T only).

name: Report the Mismatched Tiles
background: Tiles are paired from the outside inward, first with last and so on. First the number of disagreeing pairs is printed, then one line per disagreeing pair giving its left and right positions. When nothing disagrees, the output is just the single number 0.
task: Read N tile colours. Print the number of mirror pairs whose colours are unequal, then print that many lines, each containing the left and right 1-based indices (i and N+1-i) of a mismatched pair, in increasing order of i.
input_format:
Line 1: N.
Line 2: N space-separated integers.

name: Four-Way Character Split
background: Each character is sorted into at most one bucket. Vowels are a, e, i, o, u in either case; consonants are all other English letters; digits are 0-9; and punctuation means only the marks in this exact set: . , ! ? : ; - ' " ( ) [ ] { }. Anything else, such as a space, is ignored entirely.
task: Read a line of text and print four integers: the counts of vowels, consonants, digits and punctuation, in that order.
input_format: Line 1: the string S.

name: Nameplate Breakdown
background: Four separate tallies are kept: capital letters A-Z, small letters a-z, space characters, and digits 0-9. Every other character, such as a hyphen or full stop, belongs to none of these and is simply not counted.
task: Read a nameplate line and print four integers: the counts of uppercase letters, lowercase letters, spaces and digits, in that order.
input_format: Line 1: the string S.
constraints:
length of S: 1-100
S contains printable ASCII characters

name: Log Line Anatomy
background: Characters are grouped into four buckets: letters A-Z and a-z, digits 0-9, bracket characters from the set [ ] ( ) { } < >, and other printable symbols. That last bucket means any printable character that is not a letter, digit, bracket or space, so spaces themselves are never counted anywhere.
task: Read a log line and print four integers: the counts of letters, digits, brackets and other printable symbols, in that order.
input_format: Line 1: the string S.
constraints:
length of S: 1-100
S contains printable ASCII characters
bracket set: [ ] ( ) { } < >

name: Password Composition
background: A password is scored on four counts: capital letters, small letters, digits, and special characters drawn from this exact set: ! @ # $ % ^ & * ( ) - _ + =. Characters outside all four groups, such as a full stop or a space, are not counted at all.
task: Read a password string and print four integers: the counts of uppercase letters, lowercase letters, digits and special characters, in that order.
input_format: Line 1: the string S.
constraints:
length of S: 1-100
S contains printable ASCII characters
special set: ! @ # $ % ^ & * ( ) - _ + =

name: Inventory Code Audit
background: The whole code string is scanned character by character, without splitting it into tokens first. Four tallies are kept: vowels (a, e, i, o, u in either case), consonants (all other English letters), separators (commas and semicolons), and digits. Empty tokens between two separators are perfectly legal.
task: Read an inventory-code string and print four integers: the counts of vowels, consonants, separators (',' and ';') and digits, in that order.
input_format: Line 1: the string S.
constraints:
length of S: 1-100
S contains letters, digits, commas and semicolons

name: Sum the Digits
background: The digit sum adds up the individual decimal digits of a number, so 407 gives 4 + 0 + 7 = 11. A minus sign is not a digit and is ignored, meaning -407 also gives 11. The number 0 counts as the single digit 0.
task: Read an integer V, ignore any minus sign, and print the sum of its decimal digits.
input_format: Line 1: the integer V.

name: Multiply the Digits
background: The digit product multiplies the decimal digits together, so 234 gives 2 x 3 x 4 = 24. A single 0 digit anywhere drags the whole product to 0. A minus sign is ignored, and the number 0 is treated as the single digit 0.
task: Read an integer K, ignore any minus sign, and print the product of its decimal digits.
input_format: Line 1: the integer K.

name: Count a Digit
background: Only the digits actually written in the number are examined, so there are no invisible leading zeros to worry about. A minus sign is ignored. The number 0 is written as the single digit 0, so searching it for the digit 0 gives an answer of 1.
task: Read an integer ID and a digit D. Ignoring any minus sign, print how many times D appears in the decimal representation of ID.
input_format:
Line 1: the integer ID.
Line 2: the digit D.

name: Reverse the Serial
background: The digits of the number's magnitude are written back to front, and the original sign is then reattached. Any zeros that end up at the front simply vanish, because numbers are not written with leading zeros: 1200 reverses to 0021, which is just 21.
task: Read an integer S. Reverse the decimal digits of its magnitude, drop any leading zeros, and print the result carrying the original sign.
input_format: Line 1: the integer S.

name: Count the Even Digits
background: The even digits are 0, 2, 4, 6 and 8, and note that 0 counts as even. A minus sign is ignored, so only the digits themselves matter. The number 0 is a single digit 0, giving an answer of 1.
task: Read an integer P, ignore any minus sign, and print how many of its decimal digits are even.
input_format: Line 1: the integer P.

name: Even or Odd
background: A number is even when dividing it by 2 leaves no remainder, and odd otherwise. This works for negatives too: -4 is even and -3 is odd. Zero is even.
task: Read a single integer N and print EVEN if it is divisible by 2, otherwise ODD.
input_format: Line 1: the integer N.

name: Divisible by Three
background: A number is divisible by 3 when dividing it by 3 leaves a remainder of exactly zero. Negative numbers follow the same rule, so -9 is divisible by 3. Zero is divisible by 3.
task: Read a single integer N and print DIVISIBLE if N is divisible by 3, otherwise NOT DIVISIBLE.
input_format: Line 1: the integer N.

name: Inside the Window
background: The interval is inclusive, so landing exactly on either endpoint still counts as being inside. The value must be at least L and at most R simultaneously. If L is greater than R the interval is empty and nothing can be inside it.
task: Read three integers X, L and R. Print INSIDE if L <= X <= R, otherwise OUTSIDE.
input_format: Line 1: X, L, R (space-separated).

name: Leap Year Check
background: The Gregorian rule has three layers: a year divisible by 4 is a leap year, EXCEPT that years divisible by 100 are not, EXCEPT that years divisible by 400 are. So 2000 is a leap year but 1900 is not. The same arithmetic is applied to zero and negative years here.
task: Read a year Y and print LEAP if it is a Gregorian leap year, otherwise COMMON.
input_format: Line 1: the integer Y.
constraints:
|Y| up to 10^18
Y may be zero or negative

name: Classify the Sign
background: Every integer falls into exactly one of three groups: greater than zero, exactly zero, or less than zero. Zero is neither positive nor negative and gets its own answer.
task: Read a single integer N. Print POSITIVE if N > 0, ZERO if N = 0, and NEGATIVE if N < 0.
input_format: Line 1: the integer N.

name: Count the Divisors
background: A divisor of N is any positive whole number that divides N leaving no remainder. Both 1 and N itself always count. For example 12 has the divisors 1, 2, 3, 4, 6 and 12, so the answer would be 6.
task: Read a positive integer N and print how many positive divisors it has.
input_format: Line 1: the integer N.

name: List the Proper Divisors
background: A proper divisor of M is a divisor strictly smaller than M, so M itself is excluded while 1 is included. The proper divisors of 12 are 1, 2, 3, 4 and 6. The number 1 has no proper divisors at all, giving an empty line.
task: Read a positive integer M and print all its proper divisors (divisors strictly less than M) in increasing order, separated by spaces. If there are none, print an empty line.
input_format: Line 1: the integer M.

name: Smallest Real Divisor
background: Every number above 1 has a smallest divisor greater than 1, and that divisor is always a prime. For a prime number the answer is the number itself, since nothing smaller divides it. The special case X = 1 has no divisor above 1, so the answer is defined as 1.
task: Read a positive integer X and print its smallest divisor greater than 1. If X is 1, print 1.
input_format: Line 1: the integer X.

name: Sum the Proper Divisors
background: The proper divisors of A are its divisors excluding A itself, so 1 is included but A is not. For 12 those are 1, 2, 3, 4 and 6, which total 16. The number 1 has no proper divisors, so its total is 0.
task: Read a positive integer A and print the sum of all its proper divisors (excluding A itself).
input_format: Line 1: the integer A.

name: Small Divisors Only
background: Only divisors that do not exceed the bound K are counted. Since 1 divides every number, the answer is at least 1 whenever K is at least 1. Divisors larger than K are ignored even though they still divide N.
task: Read a positive integer N and a bound K. Print how many positive divisors of N are at most K.
input_format: Line 1: N, K (space-separated).

name: Scale the Elevation Map
background: A grid is a rectangle of numbers arranged in rows and columns. Scaling means every single cell is multiplied by the same factor K, independently of its neighbours. The shape of the grid never changes, only the values inside it.
task: Read an R by C grid of integers and multiply every cell by K. Print the resulting grid, one row per line with values separated by spaces.
input_format:
Line 1: R, C, K (space-separated).
Next R lines: C space-separated integers each.
constraints:
R, C: 1-20
K: -100 to 100
cell values: -1000 to 1000

name: Paint the Border
background: The border of a grid is every cell sitting in the first row, the last row, the first column or the last column. Everything else is an inner cell. In a grid with only one row or only one column, every cell is on the border.
task: Read an R by C pixel grid and replace every border cell with B, leaving inner cells unchanged. Print the modified grid.
input_format:
Line 1: R, C, B (space-separated).
Next R lines: C space-separated integers each.

name: Transpose the Matrix
background: Transposing flips a square matrix over its main diagonal, so the value in row i column j moves to row j column i. The diagonal cells, where the row and column numbers match, never move. Transposing twice returns the original matrix.
task: Read an N by N integer matrix and print its transpose, one row per line.
input_format:
Line 1: N.
Next N lines: N space-separated integers each.

name: Checkerboard Negation
background: Rows and columns are numbered starting at 1. A cell is flipped when its row number plus its column number is even, which produces a checkerboard pattern starting with the top-left cell (1+1 = 2, which is even). Negating a value simply flips its sign.
task: Read an R by C matrix and negate every cell whose row index plus column index is even (indices start at 1). Print the updated matrix.
input_format:
Line 1: R, C (space-separated).
Next R lines: C space-separated integers each.
constraints:
R, C: 1-20
row and column indices are 1-based
cell values: -1000 to 1000

name: Weight the Columns
background: Each column has its own multiplier, supplied as a list with one factor per column. Every cell in column 1 is multiplied by the first factor, every cell in column 2 by the second, and so on. Cells in the same column always share the same factor regardless of their row.
task: Read an R by C grid and a list of C column factors. Multiply every element in column j by the j-th factor and print the transformed grid.
input_format:
Line 1: R, C (space-separated).
Next R lines: C space-separated integers each.
Last line: C space-separated factors.
constraints:
R, C: 1-20
factors: -100 to 100
cell values: -1000 to 1000

name: Heaviest Row
background: Each row is reduced to a single number by adding up all the values in it, then the largest of those row totals is located. If two rows tie on total, the one nearer the top wins. Row numbers start at 1, and a grid with no rows at all answers -1.
task: Read an R by C grid and print the 1-based index of the row with the largest sum. If several rows tie, choose the smallest index. If R is 0, print -1.
input_format:
Line 1: R, C (space-separated).
Next R lines: C space-separated integers each.

name: Column Maxima
background: Each column is reduced to a single number by taking the largest value anywhere in that column, scanning down through all the rows. The results are then listed left to right, one per column. If there are no columns, the output is an empty line.
task: Read an R by C matrix and print the maximum value of each column, in left-to-right order, separated by spaces. If C is 0, print an empty line.
input_format:
Line 1: R, C (space-separated).
Next R lines: C space-separated integers each.

name: Count Walls per Row
background: The grid is drawn with two characters: a hash marks a wall and a dot marks empty space. Each row is reduced to how many walls it contains, and those counts are listed from the top row downward. A grid with no rows produces an empty line.
task: Read an R by C grid of '.' and '#' characters and print the number of '#' in each row, top to bottom, separated by spaces. If R is 0, print an empty line.
input_format:
Line 1: R, C (space-separated).
Next R lines: a string of exactly C characters, each '.' or '#'.

name: Weakest Strongest Row
background: Each row is first reduced to its own largest element. Among those row maxima, the smallest one is then located. Note the unusual tie-break: if several rows share that smallest maximum, the one nearest the BOTTOM wins. A grid with no rows answers -1.
task: Read an R by C grid. For each row compute its maximum element, then print the 1-based index of the row whose maximum is smallest. If several rows tie, choose the largest index. If R is 0, print -1.
input_format:
Line 1: R, C (space-separated).
Next R lines: C space-separated integers each.

name: Weakest Column
background: Each column is first reduced to its own largest value. Among those column maxima, the smallest one is located and its column number reported, counting from 1 on the left. Ties go to the leftmost such column, and a grid with no columns answers -1.
task: Read an R by C matrix. Compute the maximum of each column, then print the 1-based index of the column whose maximum is smallest. If several tie, choose the leftmost. If C is 0, print -1.
input_format:
Line 1: R, C (space-separated).
Next R lines: C space-separated integers each.

name: Robot on a Ledge
background: The robot walks a grid whose rows run 1 to R from the top and whose columns run 1 to C from the left. N moves up one row, S down, E right and W left. A move that would carry the robot off the edge is simply ignored, so it stays put for that step rather than wrapping around.
task: Read a grid size, a starting position and a string of moves from {N, S, E, W}. Moves that would leave the grid are ignored. Print the robot's final row and column, separated by a space.
input_format:
Line 1: R, C, r, c (space-separated).
Line 2: the move string.
constraints:
R, C: 1-100
start 1 <= r <= R, 1 <= c <= C
move string length: 1-100
moves are N, S, E or W

name: Probe on a Donut
background: This grid wraps around like the surface of a donut: stepping off the top edge brings you back on the bottom, and stepping off the right edge brings you back on the left. Rows run 1 to R and columns 1 to C. No move is ever blocked.
task: Read a grid size, a starting position and a string of moves from {N, S, E, W} on a wraparound grid. Print the probe's final row and column, separated by a space.
input_format:
Line 1: R, C, r, c (space-separated).
Line 2: the move string.
constraints:
R, C: 1-100
start 1 <= r <= R, 1 <= c <= C
move string length: 1-100
moves are N, S, E or W

name: Trace the Courier
background: Rows and columns are numbered from 0 here, so the top-left cell is (0,0) and the bottom-right is (R-1, C-1). A move that would leave the grid is ignored. Every step produces a coordinate, including blocked steps where the courier does not actually move, and the starting cell is reported first.
task: Read a grid size, a starting position and a list of moves from {N, S, E, W}. Moves that would exit the grid are ignored. Print every visited coordinate in order, including the start, one 'row col' pair per line.
input_format:
Line 1: R, C, r, c (space-separated).
Line 2: the move string.
constraints:
R, C: 1-100
row and column indices are 0-based
start 0 <= r < R, 0 <= c < C
move string length: 1-50
moves are N, S, E or W

name: How Far Did the Drone Get
background: The grid wraps around at every edge, so the drone can never be blocked. Manhattan distance measures how far apart two cells are by adding the row gap and the column gap, ignoring any wraparound: from (1,1) to (3,2) the distance is 2 + 1 = 3.
task: Read a grid size, a starting position and a string of moves from {N, S, E, W} on a wraparound grid. Print the Manhattan distance between the final position and the starting position.
input_format:
Line 1: R, C, r, c (space-separated).
Line 2: the move string.
constraints:
R, C: 1-100
start 1 <= r <= R, 1 <= c <= C
move string length: 1-100
moves are N, S, E or W

name: Cells the Painter Touched
background: The painter marks every cell it stands on, including the one it starts on. A move that would leave the grid is ignored, leaving the painter in place. Revisiting a cell does not paint it twice, so only distinct cells are counted.
task: Read a grid size, a starting position and a string of moves from {N, S, E, W}. Moves that would leave the grid are ignored. Print how many distinct cells were visited, including the start.
input_format:
Line 1: R, C, r, c (space-separated).
Line 2: the move string.
constraints:
R, C: 1-100
start 1 <= r <= R, 1 <= c <= C
move string length: 1-100
moves are N, S, E or W

name: Bank Balance Floor
background: Transactions are applied one after another in the order given, with positive values adding and negative values subtracting. The balance can never go below zero: if a withdrawal would push it negative, the balance stops at zero instead and the excess is simply lost.
task: Read a starting balance and N transactions. Apply them in order, clamping the balance to a minimum of 0 after each one. Print the final balance.
input_format:
Line 1: the starting balance and N (space-separated).
Line 2: N space-separated integers.

name: Peak Temperature
background: Adjustments are applied one at a time, positive values warming and negative values cooling. The answer is the highest temperature the thermometer ever showed at any moment, including the starting reading before any adjustment was made. There is no clamping here.
task: Read a starting temperature and N adjustments. Apply them in order and print the maximum temperature reached at any point, including the starting value.
input_format:
Line 1: the starting temperature and N (space-separated).
Line 2: N space-separated integers.
constraints:
starting temperature: -1000000 to 1000000
N: 1-100
adjustments: -1000000 to 1000000

name: First Time in the Red
background: Event deltas are applied one at a time to a running score. The answer is the position of the first event that leaves the score below zero, counting events from 1. A score of exactly zero is not negative. If the score never dips below zero, the answer is -1.
task: Read a starting score and N event deltas. Apply them in order and print the 1-based index of the first event after which the score becomes negative, or -1 if it never does.
input_format:
Line 1: the starting score and N (space-separated).
Line 2: N space-separated integers.

name: Warehouse Stock Level
background: Changes are applied one after another, positive values adding stock and negative values removing it. Stock cannot go negative: if a removal exceeds what is present, the count is clamped to zero and the shortfall is not carried forward.
task: Read a starting inventory count and N changes. Apply them in order, clamping the inventory to a minimum of 0 after each change. Print the final inventory count.
input_format:
Line 1: the starting inventory and N (space-separated).
Line 2: N space-separated integers.

name: Fuel Remaining
background: Operations are applied in sequence, positive values refuelling and negative values burning fuel. The tank can never hold less than zero: a burn larger than the remaining fuel empties the tank rather than creating a negative reading.
task: Read a starting fuel amount and N operations. Apply them in order, clamping fuel to a minimum of 0 after each one. Print the remaining fuel level.
input_format:
Line 1: the starting fuel and N (space-separated).
Line 2: N space-separated integers.

name: Sort by the Given Order
background: Instead of the usual numeric order, a custom order is supplied as a list naming every distinct value exactly once. A value's rank is its position in that list, so the first listed value comes first in the output. Duplicates in the array simply group together.
task: Read N integers and an ordering list P containing each distinct value exactly once. Reorder the array so its elements follow the order given by P, and print the result.
input_format:
Line 1: N.
Line 2: N space-separated integers.
Line 3: M, the length of P.
Line 4: M space-separated integers.
constraints:
N: 1-100
M: 1-100
P contains every distinct value of the array exactly once

name: Sort by an Alien Alphabet
background: Words are compared letter by letter as usual, but letter order comes from a supplied permutation of the alphabet rather than a-to-z. Whichever letter appears earlier in that permutation is considered smaller. If one word is a prefix of another, the shorter word comes first.
task: Read N lowercase words and a custom alphabet (a permutation of the 26 letters). Sort the words by that alphabet's lexicographic order and print them.
input_format:
Line 1: N.
Line 2: N space-separated lowercase words.
Line 3: a 26-letter permutation of the alphabet.
constraints:
N: 1-100
words: 1-20 lowercase letters
alphabet line is always a permutation of all 26 letters

name: Sort Names by Length
background: Names are ordered by how many characters they contain, either shortest first (ASC) or longest first (DESC). The sort is stable, meaning names of equal length keep the relative order they had in the input, and this applies in both directions.
task: Read N names and a direction token (ASC or DESC). Sort the names by length in that direction, keeping the original relative order among names of equal length. Print the sorted names.
input_format:
Line 1: N.
Line 2: N space-separated names.
Line 3: ASC or DESC.

name: Sort by First-Letter Priority
background: Only the very first character of each code matters. A priority string lists characters in the order they should rank, so a code beginning with the earliest-listed character comes first. The sort is stable, so codes sharing a first character keep their input order.
task: Read N product codes and a priority string listing characters in rank order. Sort the codes by the rank of their first character, keeping the input order among ties. Print the sorted list.
input_format:
Line 1: N.
Line 2: N space-separated codes.
Line 3: the priority string.
constraints:
N: 1-100
codes: 1-20 characters, non-empty
the priority string contains every possible first character exactly once

name: Reorder to the Standard Ranking
background: A ranked list defines the official order of the colour names. Each colour's rank is its position in that list, and the input sequence is rearranged to follow it. Repeated colours simply group together at their rank.
task: Read N colour names and a ranked list defining the standard order. Reorder the input colours to follow that ranking exactly and print the reordered list.

Line 2: N space-separated colour names.
Line 3: M, the length of the ranked list.
Line 4: M space-separated colour names.
constraints:
N: 1-100
M: 1-100
the ranked list contains every colour appearing in the input

name: Build an Arithmetic Run
background: An arithmetic sequence starts at some value and adds a fixed step to get each following term. With start 2 and step 3 the terms run 2, 5, 8, 11 and so on. The step may be zero (every term identical) or negative (the sequence counts down).
task: Read three integers N, S and D. Build a sequence of length N whose i-th term (1-based) equals S + (i-1) x D, and print the N integers separated by spaces.
input_format: Line 1: N, S, D (space-separated).

name: Alternate Two Values
background: The sequence flips back and forth between two values based on position, with positions counted from 1. Odd positions take X and even positions take Y, so the pattern reads X, Y, X, Y and so on. The two values may be equal.
task: Read three integers N, X and Y. Build a sequence of length N where the i-th element (1-based) is X when i is odd and Y when i is even. Print the N values.
input_format: Line 1: N, X, Y (space-separated).
constraints:
N: 1-100
X, Y: -10000 to 10000
positions are 1-based

name: Repeat the Pattern
background: A short pattern is tiled over and over until the required length is reached. When the pattern runs out it starts again from its first element. The final repetition may be cut off partway if N is not a multiple of the pattern length.
task: Read integers N and K followed by K pattern values. Build a sequence of length N by repeating the pattern, and print the N numbers.
input_format:
Line 1: N, K (space-separated).
Line 2: K space-separated integers.

name: Pronic Numbers
background: Each term multiplies a counter by the next number up, so term 1 is 1 x 2 = 2, term 2 is 2 x 3 = 6, and term 3 is 3 x 4 = 12. These are sometimes called pronic or oblong numbers. The counter always starts at 1.
task: Read an integer N and build the sequence whose i-th term equals i x (i+1) for i from 1 to N. Print the N values in order.
input_format: Line 1: N.

name: Staircase Sequence
background: The sequence holds a value steady for R positions, then jumps by D, holds for another R positions, and so on, producing a staircase. With R = 2, start 5 and step 3 the terms run 5, 5, 8, 8, 11, 11. The final step may be incomplete.
task: Read integers N, R, S and D. Build a sequence of length N whose i-th term (1-based) equals S + floor((i-1)/R) x D, so the value increases by D every R positions. Print the N integers.
input_format: Line 1: N, R, S, D (space-separated).

name: Running Total
background: A running sum reports the total so far at every step rather than just the final answer. For [1, 2, 3] the running sums are 1, then 1+2 = 3, then 1+2+3 = 6. The output always has exactly as many numbers as the input.
task: Read N integers and print the running sum after each element: the total of the first i elements, for i from 1 to N.
input_format:
Line 1: N.
Line 2: N space-separated integers.

name: Best So Far
background: A running maximum reports the highest value seen up to each point. Once a new record appears the reported value rises and then never falls again, so the output is always nondecreasing. For [3, 1, 5] the running maxima are 3, 3, 5.
task: Read N game scores and print, for every prefix, the maximum score seen so far.
input_format:
Line 1: N.
Line 2: N space-separated integers.

name: Running Parity
background: Parity records whether a running total is even (0) or odd (1). Each new 1 flips the parity and each 0 leaves it unchanged. For [1, 1, 0] the parities run 1, 0, 0.
task: Read N binary values and print, for every prefix, the parity of the sum so far (that is, the running total modulo 2).
input_format:
Line 1: N.
Line 2: N space-separated bits, each 0 or 1.

name: Running Divisible Count
background: At every step the output reports how many elements so far are divisible by K, that is, leave no remainder when divided by K. The count never decreases as more elements are read. Zero is divisible by every K.
task: Read an integer K and N values. For every prefix, print how many of the first i elements are divisible by K.
input_format:
Line 1: N, K (space-separated).
Line 2: N space-separated integers.

name: Running Above-Threshold Count
background: At every step the output reports how many elements so far are strictly greater than T, so a value exactly equal to T is never counted. The count never decreases as more elements arrive.
task: Read a threshold T and N values. For every prefix, print how many of the first i elements are strictly greater than T.
input_format:
Line 1: N, T (space-separated).
Line 2: N space-separated integers.

name: Title Case the Line
background: The line is split into tokens wherever spaces occur, and runs of several spaces act as a single divider. Each token then has its first character made uppercase and every other letter made lowercase. Punctuation stays attached to whatever token it sits in, and tokens are rejoined with exactly one space.
task: Read a line of text whose tokens are separated by one or more spaces. Capitalise the first character of each token and lowercase the rest, then print the tokens joined by single spaces.
input_format: Line 1: the text line.
constraints:
line length: 1-200
tokens are separated by one or more spaces
no leading or trailing spaces

name: Reverse Each Token
background: The line is split into tokens on spaces, treating several spaces in a row as one divider. Each token's characters are then written back to front, but the tokens themselves stay in their original order. Punctuation travels with its token and gets reversed along with it.
task: Read a line of text whose tokens are separated by one or more spaces. Reverse the characters of each token independently, then print the tokens joined by single spaces.
input_format: Line 1: the text line.
constraints:
line length: 1-200
tokens are separated by one or more spaces
no leading or trailing spaces

name: Swap a Word
background: Only tokens that match A exactly and completely are replaced, and the comparison is case-sensitive so 'Cat' does not match 'cat'. A token that merely contains A as part of a longer word is left alone. Several spaces in a row count as a single divider.
task: Read a line of text and two words A and B. Replace every token exactly equal to A with B (case-sensitive), leave other tokens unchanged, and print the tokens joined by single spaces.
input_format:
Line 1: the text line.
Line 2: A and B, separated by a space.
constraints:
line length: 1-200
A and B: 1-20 characters, no spaces
tokens are separated by one or more spaces
no leading or trailing spaces
sample_input:
the cat sat on the cat
cat dog
sample_output: the dog sat on the dog
test1_input:
the cat sat on the cat
cat dog
test1_output: the dog sat on the dog
test8_input:
aa aa aa aa
aa bb

name: Number the Tokens
background: Each token gets an underscore and its position appended, with positions counted from 1. So the first token becomes token_1, the second token_2, and so on. Multiple spaces act as a single divider, so they do not create empty tokens or skip numbers.
task: Read a line of text whose tokens are separated by one or more spaces. Append _k to each token, where k is its 1-based position, then print the tokens joined by single spaces.
input_format: Line 1: the text line.
constraints:
line length: 1-200
tokens are separated by one or more spaces
no leading or trailing spaces

name: Shout the Line
background: Every letter is converted to uppercase while digits and punctuation are unaffected. The line is split on spaces with runs of spaces treated as one divider, and the tokens are rejoined with exactly one space between them.
task: Read a line of text whose tokens are separated by one or more spaces. Convert every token to uppercase, then print the tokens joined by single spaces.
input_format: Line 1: the text line.
constraints:
line length: 1-200
tokens are separated by one or more spaces
no leading or trailing spaces

name: First Circular Twin
background: The array is treated as a closed ring, so the element after the last one is the first one again. Indices start at 0. The search looks for the earliest position whose neighbour on the ring holds the same value, which includes the wraparound pair of last-and-first.
task: Read N integers treated as a circular array. Print the smallest 0-based index i such that a[i] equals a[(i+1) mod N], or -1 if no such index exists.
input_format:
Line 1: N.
Line 2: N space-separated integers.

name: Count the Circular Climbs
background: Every position is compared with the position K steps ahead of it, wrapping around the end of the array back to the start. Indices start at 0. The answer counts how many of those comparisons find the value ahead to be strictly larger.
task: Read N integers and an offset K. Print how many indices i satisfy a[(i+K) mod N] > a[i].
input_format:
Line 1: N, K (space-separated).
Line 2: N space-separated integers.
constraints:
N: 1-100
K: 0 to N-1
indices are 0-based
values: -10000 to 10000

name: Read the Ring
background: The string is arranged in a circle so that after the last character comes the first again. Starting at position P (counted from 0) and walking forward one step at a time, exactly N characters are read, which produces a rotation of the original string.
task: Read a string of length N and a start position P. Print the N characters obtained by walking forward from P with wraparound.
input_format:
Line 1: the string S.
Line 2: P.
constraints:
length of S: 1-100
P: 0 to N-1
positions are 0-based

name: Find a Circular Peak
background: The array wraps into a ring, so the first element's left neighbour is the last element and vice versa. A peak is strictly greater than BOTH of its ring neighbours. Indices start at 0, and when several peaks exist the smallest index is reported.
task: Read N integers treated as a circular array. Print the smallest 0-based index i where a[i] is strictly greater than both a[(i-1) mod N] and a[(i+1) mod N], or -1 if no such index exists.
input_format:
Line 1: N.
Line 2: N space-separated integers.

name: Pair Each with Its Jump
background: Every element is paired with whatever sits K steps ahead of it on the ring, wrapping past the end back to the start. Indices start at 0 and one pair is produced for each position. Pairs are written with no spaces inside the brackets.
task: Read N integers and a jump K. Print the N pairs (a[i], a[(i+K) mod N]) for i from 0 to N-1, each written as (x,y) with no internal spaces, separated by single spaces.
input_format:
Line 1: N, K (space-separated).
Line 2: N space-separated integers.
constraints:
N: 1-100
K: 0 to N-1
indices are 0-based
values: -10000 to 10000

name: Add Two Arrays
background: Two arrays of the same length are combined position by position: the first element of one is added to the first element of the other, the second to the second, and so on. No element is ever combined with one at a different position.
task: Read two arrays A and B of N integers each and print the array C where C[i] = A[i] + B[i].
input_format:
Line 1: N.
Line 2: N space-separated integers (array A).
Line 3: N space-separated integers (array B).

name: Subtract Two Readings
background: Two equal-length sequences are combined position by position, subtracting the second from the first at each index. Order matters here, since subtraction is not symmetric: 3 minus 5 is -2, not 2.
task: Read two sequences T and U of N integers each and print the sequence D where D[i] = T[i] - U[i].
input_format:
Line 1: N.
Line 2: N space-separated integers (sequence T).
Line 3: N space-separated integers (sequence U).

name: Match Mask
background: Two strings of equal length are compared one character position at a time. Each position produces a single digit: 1 when the two characters are identical and 0 when they differ. The comparison is case-sensitive.
task: Read two equal-length strings S and T. Print a binary string R where R[i] is '1' if S[i] equals T[i] and '0' otherwise.
input_format:
Line 1: the string S.
Line 2: the string T.
constraints:
length of S and T: 1-100, always equal
both strings contain English letters only

name: Stronger of Each Pair
background: Two equal-length lists are compared position by position, and at each index the larger of the two values is kept. When the two values are equal, that shared value is kept.
task: Read two lists H1 and H2 of N positive integers each and print the list M where M[i] = max(H1[i], H2[i]).
input_format:
Line 1: N.
Line 2: N space-separated integers (list H1).
Line 3: N space-separated integers (list H2).

name: Zip Two Strings
background: Two equal-length strings are woven together character by character: the first character of one, then the first of the other, then the second of each, and so on. The result is twice as long as either input.
task: Read two equal-length strings A and B and print the interleaved string A[1]B[1]A[2]B[2]...A[N]B[N].
input_format:
Line 1: the string A.
Line 2: the string B.
constraints:
length of A and B: 1-100, always equal
both strings contain English letters only
